The early street is not yet awake. A baker unlocks his door, and warm light spills across wet stones. Somewhere above, a curtain moves. A cat watches pigeons argue over crumbs. The world feels unfinished, as if night has only folded itself into a corner, waiting for voices to unfold it again.

I like this hour because nothing demands an answer. Messages sleep in pockets. Trains yawn along iron ribs. Even the river seems to slow, carrying reflections of lamps like coins it cannot spend. A woman walks a dog that stops to greet every shadow. An old man reads a newspaper upside down, perhaps joking with the dawn.

There is a kindness in ordinary beginnings. The sun does not announce itself with trumpets. It leans over rooftops, tests the air, then paints the windows gold. Birds rehearse their opinions. Buses cough at stops. A child presses her face to glass, fascinated by the way the city gathers itself.

I think of all the lives beginning simultaneously: tea poured, shoelaces tied, prayers whispered, alarms silenced. Each person carries a private weather. Some are brave, some tired, some hopeful without knowing why.

By the time the shops raise their shutters, the spell softens. Yet I keep a fragment of that quiet in my pocket. It reminds me that before the world becomes loud, it is gently made. I hope to remember this fragile hour whenever noise rises, because stillness teaches the heart how to notice grace again each day more often.
